classification.habit: Much-branched, spiny, woody climber with tuberous fasciculated roots.
classification.habitat: Tropical and subtropical forests, scrub and hedges, ascending the hills to about 1,500 m.
classification.distribution: Throughout India, including the Himalaya and the peninsular forests; widely cultivated.

identification.description: Much-branched, spiny, woody climber with tufts of needle-like cladodes in place of leaves, small white fragrant flowers, red berries and numerous fasciculated spindle-shaped tuberous roots.
identification.whole_plant: Climbing shrub with slender grooved branches, recurved spines and tufts of needle-like cladodes instead of true leaves, bearing numerous spindle-shaped root tubers.
identification.root: Numerous fasciculated, fusiform tuberous roots, 10–30 cm long, tapering at both ends, cream coloured with longitudinal wrinkles; taste sweetish (API).
identification.stem: Woody, whitish-grey, grooved stem with stout straight or recurved spines at the nodes.
identification.leaf: True leaves reduced to scales or spines; green, linear, curved cladodes 1–2.5 cm long occur in tufts of 2–6.
identification.flower: Small, white, fragrant flowers in simple or branched racemes.
identification.fruit: Globose berries, about 5 mm across, turning red when ripe.
identification.seed: One to few hard, black seeds per berry.
identification_points: Cream-coloured, wrinkled root with sweetish taste

therapeutics.precautions: Guru and Snigdha drug: use cautiously in Mandagni, Ama and Kapha-predominant states and in obesity. Use authenticated root; peeled, dried root is the standard drug.
therapeutics.contraindications: Ama with weak digestion, Kaphaja disorders with heaviness, and hormone-sensitive conditions without medical advice; known allergy to Asparagus.

shlokas:
शतावरी बहुसुता भीरुरिन्दीवरी वरी ।
नारायणी शतपदी शतवीर्या च पीवरी ॥
शतावरी गुरुः शीता तिक्तास्वाद्वी रसायनी ।
मेधाग्निपुष्टिदा स्निग्धा नेत्र्या गुल्मातिसारजित् ।
शुक्रस्तन्यकरी बल्या वातपित्तास्रशोथजित् ॥

phytochemistry.chemical_notes: The root is rich in steroidal saponins (shatavarins based on sarsasapogenin) with sugars and mucilage, matching its Madhura-Snigdha profile.

modern_information.evidence_summary: Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) supports female reproductive health, boosts vitality, and is a top Ayurvedic rejuvenator for Pitta and Vata.
recognized_uses: Galactagogue and female reproductive tonic in traditional practice
modern_information.safety_notes: Generally well tolerated at usual doses; mild gastrointestinal upset may occur. Data in pregnancy are limited, so use only on medical advice.

Rasa: Madhura, Tikta; Guna: Guru, Snigdha; Virya: Sheeta; Vipaka: Madhura
Karma: Rasayana, Stanyajanana, Shukrala, Vrishya, Balya, Medhya
Charaka: Balya, Vayahsthapana and Madhura skandha
Formulations: Shatavari Guda, Shatavari Ghrita, Brahma Rasayana

Which part of Shatavari is used and how is it identified?
Why is Shatavari called a Stanyajanana and Rasayana dravya?

student.quick_revision: Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus): tuberous root; Madhura-Tikta rasa, Guru-Snigdha guna, Sheeta virya, Madhura vipaka; Vata-Pitta shamaka; Rasayana, Stanyajanana, Vrishya, Medhya.

teaching_points: Explain cladodes as modified stems replacing leaves.
Correlate Madhura-Sheeta-Guru profile with Pittahara and Brimhana action.
Discuss Shatavari as a Stanyajanana and female Rasayana.
discussion_points: Classical Rasayana claims versus modern evidence on galactagogue action
practical_points: Examine fresh and dried roots: shape, colour, wrinkles and sweetish taste.
Show a herbarium twig with cladodes and spines.

doctor.quick_reference: Shatavari root (Madhura-Tikta, Sheeta, Madhura vipaka) is a Rasayana, Stanyajanana and Pittahara drug used in Stanyakshaya, Amlapitta and Shukrakshaya; given with milk or ghee.
key_precautions: Use cautiously in Mandagni and Ama
Use cautiously in Kapha disorders and obesity
Use in pregnancy only on medical advice
